primary.thesis: As of 2026-09-30, Maduro is in US custody after the January 2026 US operation. Delcy Rodríguez, the executive vice president, was sworn in as acting/encargada president under the constitution's vacancy provisions. The US has chosen to work through her rump chavista government, pressing it on oil access, prisoner releases and cooperation instead of installing the opposition. So the state that the UN recognizes still names her as head of state. A formal handover needs a newly called election, a count and an inauguration, and that is very unlikely to finish before Dec 31, 2026. On that path, the person who officially holds the office at noon ET on Dec 31 is still Delcy Rodríguez. Opposition figures, US officials and the detained Maduro do not meet the 'officially holds' test.

basket.reason: She is the sitting acting head of state under the constitution. Official Venezuelan government communications and the UN protocol list name her. The status quo holds unless there is a discrete break before Dec 31.

Maduro is detained abroad and facing US prosecution. The government that actually runs the country has treated the office as filled by an acting successor, so he does not 'officially hold' it on Dec 31.
For Machado to take office, a new election would have to be called, held, certified and followed by an inauguration within about 3 months. Being named or designated does not count under the rules.

The 2024 claim of González is not recognized by the government in control or by the UN protocol list. Swearing him in would need a regime-level concession that the US-Rodríguez arrangement has so far avoided.

failure_narrative: The basket loses mainly on C3, in one of two ways. (a) Washington loses patience with Rodríguez over oil terms, the pace of political prisoner releases or elections, and forces a quick handover. The National Assembly or a negotiated transition statute installs an opposition figure (Machado, or González as the 2024 claimed winner) or a caretaker, sworn in before Dec 31, and the UN listing updates. (b) An internal chavista fracture removes her, for example Cabello or Padrino López moving against her through a military or party power play, or Jorge Rodríguez taking the post in a reshuffle. That would leave another person, or a disputed situation, as official head of state on Dec 31. A smaller risk is that the resolver treats the 'acting' title as not 'officially holding' the office. That could shift resolution to the UN list, and possibly to Maduro if the UN never updated its protocol entry, which would lose C3 and C5 together.
hedge_thesis: The main failure path is a fast, US-pushed handover from Rodríguez's interim chavista state to an opposition or technocratic government. That would bring wholesale sanctions relief, a clear route to a Venezuela/PDVSA debt restructuring backed by the IMF, and a full opening of the oil sector to Western majors. Mechanically, a new government with US and UN recognition could sign restructuring deals and upstream contracts that creditors and oil companies can enforce. The interim Rodríguez government cannot do that credibly, because its legitimacy and legal standing stay contingent. So in exactly the worlds where Rodríguez is out by Dec 31, defaulted Venezuelan sovereign and PDVSA bonds should rally sharply. The Citgo/PDVSA creditor fight changes character as a recognized government comes to the table. Expected Venezuelan heavy-crude supply growth should also lean against heavy-sour differentials and help US Gulf Coast complex refiners and Chevron-type operators. If she stays, those bonds and supply expectations stay capped by the uncertainty of an interim regime.
